questions.explanation: The cells at 2, 0, 3, 1, and 4 all fall under the minimum of 5, so 5 of the 8 cells violate the rule, while 7, 11, and 6 clear it. Counting only the zeros, or treating a count of 4 as safe because it is close to 5, both read the rule as a limit rather than a floor. The threshold exists because a cell holding only a handful of records points at identifiable people, so any value under 5 is the problem.
questions.hint: Check every value against the minimum and count each one that falls short.
questions.learningObjective: count cells that fall below a small-cell disclosure threshold

questions.explanation: The records in the county file that the partner's file lacks are the 4,200 minus the 4,120 they share, which is 80. Subtracting the two file totals gives 10 and is wrong, because it compares counts without accounting for the overlap, and the larger file cannot be treated as containing the smaller. Differencing two releases like this is a standard attack: whatever a partner's table omits becomes identifiable once the totals are published.
questions.hint: Take the records in the first file and remove the ones both files share.
questions.learningObjective: compute a set difference between two overlapping releases

questions.explanation: Consent is given for a stated purpose, so patients who agreed to research for their own hospital have not agreed to a drug trial run by an outside university, and the new use needs fresh permission or a different legal basis. Consent for one purpose does not stretch to every research purpose, and an institution's status as research does not exempt it. Consent also does not dissolve when the data changes hands, since the duty follows the data.
questions.hint: Ask whether the new use was among the purposes people were told about.

questions.explanation: Privacy here comes from making the identifying combination too coarse to single anyone out, and widening the ZIP, coarsening the birth year to a decade, and suppressing thin cells each break one leg of that combination. Coding names leaves every quasi-identifier intact, so the risk survives, and removing only sex still leaves birth year plus ZIP able to pin down a person in a small area. Dropping nothing assumes the research question needs more granularity than it can justify.
questions.hint: Ask which fields, taken together, could match a single resident.
questions.learningObjective: design a release that minimizes re-identification risk

options.text: Replace names with numeric IDs, since coding alone makes records safe

options.text: Drop the sex field only, since birth year and ZIP are broad enough

options.misconception: assumes maximum detail is needed and privacy cost is irrelevant

questions.explanation: A released value can identify someone all by itself: one person in the table earns 187,432 dollars, so a colleague who knows that figure now knows who it is, and no name was ever printed. That is a memorability risk, and it is why distinctive values get banded or suppressed. The value being a number rather than a name is exactly what makes it look safe, and rounding decimals does nothing about a value whose uniqueness is the whole problem.
questions.hint: Ask how many people in the table share that exact value.
questions.learningObjective: spot a memorability disclosure in a nameless release

options.text: There is no problem, because the table publishes no names at all

options.misconception: believes a numeric value cannot carry identifying information
options.text: There is no problem, because the value is a number rather than a name

options.misconception: reduces the issue to formatting rather than to uniqueness
options.text: The problem is only the number of decimals, which should be rounded off

answer.exemplar: A signature records that a form was signed, not that the person understood what would happen, and it says nothing about whether they could decline without losing care. Real consent needs plain language, a real choice, and a warning about who will see the data and for how long, so a signature on a dense page is evidence of a procedure rather than evidence of understanding.

questions.explanation: A strong response distinguishes a signed form from genuine understanding, names comprehension, voluntariness, and the absence of consequences for declining as the parts a signature cannot show, and notes that specific harms to the person are what the consent is meant to prevent.
questions.hint: Ask what a signature actually records about the person's understanding.
questions.learningObjective: explain why a signature is not the same as informed consent
